Assume the Axiom of Choice (AC) [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\in\mathbb N_0})$ be a discrete filtration
on a measurable space, and let $\mathcal P_0$ be a family of probability laws
on $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$. A real-valued process $E=(E_t)_{t\in\mathbb N_0}$ is
a **nonnegative test supermartingale for $\mathcal P_0$** if, for every
$P\in\mathcal P_0$, it is adapted and integrable under $P$
[[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]]
[[def-martingale-submartingale-and-supermartingale]], satisfies
$P(E_t\ge0)=1$ for every $t$, and has $\mathbb E_P E_0\le1$.

The same process must satisfy the supermartingale condition under every law
in the null family; that is what makes the definition uniform over a composite
null. The initial value may be random and need not be bounded by one
pointwise. Time starts at zero.

If $X$ is adapted and $B\subseteq\mathbb R$ is Borel, then
$$\tau=\inf\{n\ge0:X_n\in B\},\qquad \inf\varnothing=\infty,$$
is a stopping time.

For a filtration $(\mathcal F_n)_{n\ge0}$, a map
$$\tau:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$$
is a **stopping time** if $\{\tau\le n\}\in\mathcal F_n$ for every $n\ge0$. It is **bounded** if some deterministic $N$ satisfies $\tau\le N$ almost surely, and **finite** if $P(\tau<\infty)=1$. These notions are distinct: finite does not mean bounded.

The event condition is literal, not merely modulo null sets; no completion of the filtration is assumed. Measurability as an extended-integer-valued random variable follows from the equivalent event tests below.

Assume AC. If $M$ is a martingale and $\sigma\le\tau$ are stopping times bounded by a deterministic $N$, then
$$\mathbb E[M_\tau\mid\mathcal F_\sigma]=M_\sigma\quad\text{a.s.},$$
so $\mathbb EM_\tau=\mathbb EM_\sigma$. For a submartingale $X$ the conditional and expectation inequalities point upward; for a supermartingale they point downward.

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let $A\in\mathcal F$.
Then the indicator $\mathbf 1_A$ satisfies
$$\mathbb E[\mathbf 1_A]=\mathbb P(A).$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Define $\tau_a=\inf\{t\ge0:M_t\ge a\}$, with $\inf\varnothing=\infty$, and $A_N=\{\tau_a\le N\}=\{\max_{0\le t\le N}M_t\ge a\}$. By [F1], $M$ is adapted; applying [F2] with the Borel set $[a,\infty)$ makes $\tau_a$ a stopping time. Thus $\tau_a\wedge N$ and the constant time $0$ are bounded stopping times, with $0\le\tau_a\wedge N$.
Apply [F4] to $0\le\tau_a\wedge N$ to get $\mathbb E_PM_{\tau_a\wedge N}\le\mathbb E_PM_0\le1$.
On $A_N$, $\tau_a\wedge N=\tau_a$ and $M_{\tau_a}\ge a$; on $A_N^c$, $\tau_a\wedge N=N$ and $M_N\ge0$ almost surely by [F1]. Hence $M_{\tau_a\wedge N}\ge a\mathbf1_{A_N}$ almost surely.
By [F5] and step 2.1, $aP(A_N)=\mathbb E_P[a\mathbf1_{A_N}]\le\mathbb E_PM_{\tau_a\wedge N}\le\mathbb E_PM_0\le1$. Dividing by $a>0$ proves both bounds.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement is vacuous when the null family is empty because there is no P in the quantified family.
The Statement and step 3.1 remain valid when E_P[M_0]=0; the right-hand probability bound is then zero.
The Statement allows N=0 and every a>0; step 1.1 includes time zero in the finite maximum.
Step 1.1 covers a process that never reaches a, with tau_a=infinity and A_N empty.

boundaries.reason: The only threshold assumption is a>0; there is no endpoint parameter in the Statement.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 1.1 and 2.1 identify AC's uses through the test-supermartingale and bounded optional-sampling suppliers.

boundaries.reason: The lemma is a one-way probability inequality, not an equivalence.
The lemma is a one-way probability inequality, not an equivalence.

risk_review.notes: Independently checked all four proof steps against F1–F5 and A1. First hitting [a,infinity) is a stopping time; its truncation and 0 are bounded by N, so the published optional-sampling supermartingale inequality applies with AC. The stopped value is integrable (finite sum of integrable M_t), at least a on A_N, and nonnegative a.s. off A_N. Indicator expectation and monotonicity give the sharper E_P M_0/a bound, including N=0 and zero initial mean. Empty null family is vacuous; a=0 is excluded. No infinite-horizon stopping or attained supremum is assumed. Reader and refuter evidence reveal no defect in this lemma; no new choice use.

$M=(M_t)_{t\in\mathbb N_0}$ be a nonnegative test supermartingale for
$\mathcal P_0$. For every $P\in\mathcal P_0$, every $a>0$, and every
$N\in\mathbb N_0$,
$$P\!\left(\max_{0\le t\le N}M_t\ge a\right)\le \frac{\mathbb E_PM_0}{a}\le\frac1a.$$

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

No finiteness hypothesis is required.

derivations.claim: For any $\gamma\in(0,1)$, set $\tau_\gamma=\inf\{t\ge0:M_t\ge1/\gamma\}$ and $A_N=\{\tau_\gamma\le N\}=\{\max_{0\le t\le N}M_t\ge1/\gamma\}$. The events $A_N$ increase and their union is $\{\tau_\gamma<\infty\}=\{\exists t\ge0:M_t\ge1/\gamma\}$.
By [F1], $P(A_N)\le\gamma$ for each $N$; [F2] gives $P(\tau_\gamma<\infty)=\lim_NP(A_N)\le\gamma$.

Put $\gamma_n=\alpha+(1-\alpha)/(n+1)$ for $n\ge1$. Then $\gamma_n\downarrow\alpha$ and $1/\gamma_n<1/\alpha$. The countable-supremum event $H=\{\sup_{t\ge0}M_t\ge1/\alpha\}$ equals $\bigcap_{n\ge1}\{\tau_{\gamma_n}<\infty\}$: if the supremum is at least $1/\alpha$, each strictly lower threshold $1/\gamma_n$ is exceeded by some process value; conversely, crossing every such threshold forces the supremum to be at least their limit $1/\alpha$. Thus $H$ is measurable and, by step 2.1, $P(H)\le\gamma_n$ for every $n$.
Letting $n\to\infty$ in step 3.1 gives $P(H)\le\alpha$. Taking $\gamma=\alpha$ in step 2.1 also gives $P(\tau_\alpha<\infty)\le\alpha$.

For a discrete stopping time $\sigma$, $\{\sigma<\infty,M_\sigma\ge1/\alpha\}=\bigcup_{t\ge0}(\{\sigma=t\}\cap\{M_t\ge1/\alpha\})\subseteq\{\tau_\alpha<\infty\}$. The event is measurable by [F3]–[F4], and step 4.1 bounds its probability by $\alpha$.

The finite-horizon supplier in steps 1.1–2.1 covers zero initial expectation and yields zero crossing probability.

Steps 1.1–2.1 cover the no-crossing case tau_gamma=infinity.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

For a filtration $(\mathcal F_n)_{n\ge0}$, a map
$$\tau:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb N_0\cup\{\infty\}$$
is a **stopping time** if $\{\tau\le n\}\in\mathcal F_n$ for every $n\ge0$. It is **bounded** if some deterministic $N$ satisfies $\tau\le N$ almost surely, and **finite** if $P(\tau<\infty)=1$. These notions are distinct: finite does not mean bounded.

The event condition is literal, not merely modulo null sets; no completion of the filtration is assumed. Measurability as an extended-integer-valued random variable follows from the equivalent event tests below.

Assume AC. Let $\mathcal P_0$ be a family of probability laws and let
$M=(M_t)_{t\in\mathbb N_0}$ be a nonnegative test supermartingale for
$\mathcal P_0$. For every $P\in\mathcal P_0$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$, define
$$\tau_\alpha=\inf\{t\ge0:M_t\ge1/\alpha\},\qquad\inf\varnothing=\infty.$$
Then
$$P\!\left(\sup_{t\ge0}M_t\ge\frac1\alpha\right)\le\alpha,\qquad P(\tau_\alpha<\infty)\le\alpha.$$
Moreover, for every discrete stopping time $\sigma$,
$$P(\sigma<\infty,\ M_\sigma\ge1/\alpha)\le\alpha,$$
where the event involving $M_\sigma$ is restricted to $\{\sigma<\infty\}$.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that

itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: For each $i$, the uniform-law assumption gives $P_0(P_i>\alpha)=1-\alpha$.

Define $\sigma=\inf\{1\le i\le K:P_i\le\alpha\}$, with $\inf\varnothing=\infty$. For every $k\ge0$, $\{\sigma\le k\}=\bigcup_{i=1}^{\min(k,K)}\{P_i\le\alpha\}\in\mathcal F_k$, where the union is empty for $k=0$. Thus [F3] makes $\sigma$ a stopping time, and the rejection event by look $K$ is $\{\sigma\le K\}$.
By [F1]–[F2], the probability that every look misses is the product of the marginal probabilities, so $P_0(\bigcap_{i=1}^K\{P_i>\alpha\})=(1-\alpha)^K$.
The event of at least one rejection is the complement of the event in step 2.1. Therefore its probability is $1-(1-\alpha)^K$.
Since $0<1-\alpha<1$ and $K\ge2$, $(1-\alpha)^K<1-\alpha$, so step 3.1 is strictly greater than $\alpha$.

[F4] controls arbitrary threshold stopping only when its nonnegative test-supermartingale hypotheses hold. The calculation above concerns repeated fixed-look uniform p-values and does not assume such a process, so the excess rejection probability is not a violation of Ville's inequality.

boundaries.reason: The example assumes an integer K>=2 and includes at least two looks.
The level alpha is restricted to (0,1), excluding zero.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement requires K>=2; step 3.1's formula would equal alpha for the excluded one-look boundary K=1.

boundaries.reason: Every look has a continuous uniform null law; no degenerate p-value law is assumed.
boundaries.evidence: Step 1.2 uses inf(empty)=infinity, has an empty stopping-time event at k=0, and freezes the union and filtration for k>=K, including paths with no rejection.

citations.quote: A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

Assume AC for the supplied existence theorem. Write $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ for the unique class in $L^1(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ consisting of conditional-expectation versions of $X$. A chosen real $\mathcal G$-measurable representative is a **version**. Equalities and inequalities involving these classes mean almost-sure equalities and inequalities.

Existence is [[thm-conditional-expectation-exists-by-radon-nikodym]] and uniqueness is [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]], applied to [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. The quotient is [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. If $X=X^{\ast}$ almost surely, [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]] gives identical event integrals, so the output class is independent of the input representative. The [[def-axiom-of-choice]] assumption is inherited from RN existence.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Assume AC [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. An integrable adapted real process $X$ [[def-adapted-and-integrable-stochastic-process]] is a **martingale**, **submartingale**, or **supermartingale** when, respectively, for every $n\ge0$,
$$E[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]=X_n,\qquad E[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]\ge X_n,\qquad E[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]\le X_n\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
These are three separate conditions, with the convention that a submartingale has conditional future mean at least its present value. The conditional expectations are the almost-sure classes of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]; that supplier inherits AC from its Radon–Nikodym existence proof. The definition itself selects no representative and assumes no completed filtration.

The condition is imposed at each adjacent pair of times. An all-pairs formulation requires a proof. No boundedness or independence is part of this definition, and no trivial or deterministic initial value is imposed.

derivations.claim: Set $p=1/4$, $c=2$, and $\Omega=\{a\}\cup\{b_k:k\ge1\}$ with $\mathcal F=2^\Omega$, $P(\{a\})=p$, and $P(\{b_k\})=(1-p)2^{-k}$. The geometric series makes $P$ a probability measure. For $n\ge0$, let $T_n=\{a\}\cup\{b_k:k>n\}$, let $\mathcal F_n$ be generated by the partition $\{\{b_1\},\ldots,\{b_n\},T_n\}$ (at $n=0$ this is the trivial partition), and put $m_n=P(T_n)=p+(1-p)2^{-n}$. These partitions refine as $n$ increases, so $(\mathcal F_n)$ is a filtration.

Define $M_n=0$ on each singleton $\{b_j\}$ with $j\le n$, and set $M_n=cp/m_n$ on $T_n$. This is $\mathcal F_n$-measurable and satisfies $0\le M_n<c$. By [F1], [F4], and [F5], $\mathbb E_PM_n\le cP(\Omega)=c<\infty$, so it is integrable.

On every revealed singleton $\{b_j\}$, $j\le n$, both $M_n$ and $M_{n+1}$ are zero. The remaining atom $T_n$ splits into $\{b_{n+1}\}$, of mass $(1-p)2^{-(n+1)}$, and $T_{n+1}$, of mass $m_{n+1}$. The conditional mean of $M_{n+1}$ on $T_n$ is $$\frac{m_{n+1}(cp/m_{n+1})+(1-p)2^{-(n+1)}\cdot0}{m_n}=\frac{cp}{m_n}=M_n,$$ since the two parts' masses sum to $m_n$. These equalities on the finitely many atoms of $\mathcal F_n$ give a conditional-expectation version by [F2]; [F3] gives its almost-sure class, and [F6] makes $M$ a martingale.
$M_0=cp=1/2$, so $\mathbb E_PM_0=cpP(\Omega)=1/2\le1$. With step 2.1 and step 3.1, [F7] shows that $M$ is a nonnegative test supermartingale for the singleton null family $\{P\}$.

Step 2.1 shows $M_n<c=2$ at every finite time, so $\tau_{1/2}=\infty$ everywhere. On $a$, $M_n=cp/[p+(1-p)2^{-n}]\to c$, so $\sup_nM_n=c$; on each $b_k$, $M_n=0$ for $n\ge k$ and the finitely many earlier values are all below $c$. Hence $\{\sup_nM_n\ge2\}=\{a\}$, with probability $1/4$, whereas $P(\tau_{1/2}<\infty)=0$. Both are at most $\alpha=1/2$, as [F8] requires, but they are not equal.

boundaries.reason: The construction has a nonempty countable sample space and singleton null family.

Counterexample 1.1 fixes p=1/4 and m_n=P(T_n)=1/4+(3/4)2^-n, hence m_n>1/4 for every finite n and m_{n+1}>0. These actual atom masses exclude zero for every denominator in 2.1 and 3.1; the initial expectation alone is not the needed exclusion.
